newsitem.title: USA: U.S. explains negative vote on Lebanon damages.
newsitem.headline: U.S. explains negative vote on Lebanon damages.

text.p: The United States said on Monday it opposed a U.N. resolution requiring Israel to pay damages resulting from the shelling of a U.N. base in Lebanon last year because the committee that took the action exceeded its authority.
"It is simply beyond the competence of the Fifth Committee to take the decisions that they took over the weekend," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told a news briefing.

"And so we are arguing on procedural grounds within the United Nations system that only the Security Council has the power and the authority to designate a country, in this case Israel ...as being responsible for paying, for being assessed with the full cost of a U.N. mission," he said.

The resolution requires that Israel pay more than $1.7 million for damages resulting from its shelling of a U.N. base at Qana in southern Lebanon last year in which about 100 civilians taking refuge were killed.

The draft, dealing with the financing of the U.N. Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), was approved on Saturday by a vote of 102 to 2 with three abstentions of the General Assembly's adminstrative and budgetary committee. The United States joined Israel in voting against the resolution.
Burns said the issue "fundamentally involves issues of international peace and security, which are the primary responsibility of the Security Council."

"If this does go to the Security Council, the United States will be very active in this debate. But we had to defend Israel, and also defend the United Nations system itself from this precedent which we believe is very unhelpful," he said.
Burns stressed that the United States strongly supports UNIFIL as a "stabilizing force in the region."
But he refused to say if Washington was threatening not to support renewal of UNIFIL, saying: "I don't want to betray the confidentiality of our diplomatic discussions."

Asked about news reports that the United States was pressuring the Lebanese government not to seek damages from Israel as a way of stopping the Israeli attacks on southern Lebanon, Burns said Lebanon's demand for compensation from Israel for the families of the victims is a separate issue and he would have to check with U.S. Middle East experts before providing an answer.
